newsitem.title: USA: Senator urges U.S. to stop Georgia aid over crash.
newsitem.headline: Senator urges U.S. to stop Georgia aid over crash.

text.p: A Republican senator urged U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday to withhold aid to Georgia until it waives immunity for a diplomat involved in a car crash in which a 16-year-old American girl was killed.

The U.S. government is expected to ask Georgia to waive immunity for the diplomat when it receives, probably on Tuesday, a formal police report on the incident. But officials hold out little hope that the waiver would be granted.
Gueorgui Makharadze, 35, a Georgian diplomat, was driving a car that started a five-car collision on Friday in which Joviane Waltrick, 16, of Kensington, Maryland, was killed.
Police have not filed any charges, but are investigating whether the diplomat was driving at an excessive speed and under the influence of alcohol.

"I believe that strong action is warranted," Senator Judd Gregg said in a letter to Clinton. "I believe the only appropriate action is for the United States to request a waiver of diplomatic immunity."
For the 1997 fiscal year, Washington expects to provide Georgia with about $30 million in financial support, he said.
"I feel that the United States should withhold this aid to Georgia until that nation sufficiently agrees to this waiver," the New Hampshire senator said.
"Americans will not tolerate having their dollars go to a nation which would use a legal technicality to harbour a drunk driver whose actions have lead to this tragic death," he said.

A spokesman at Georgia's embassy in Washington had no comment on Gregg's letter. Any decisions on immunity would not be made at the embassy but would be a decision between the two governments, Micha Siamashvili, the embassy spokesman said.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze and Makharadze each sent letters of condolence to the family of the dead girl.

As a diplomat, Makharadze is immune from prosecution. But the United States generally asks governments to waive immunity in cases of serious crimes committed by foreign diplomats in this country and is expected to do so in this case.

If the affected government does not grant immunity, the common practice is for the United States to ask that the diplomat leave the country and he is not permitted to return, unless he submits to prosecution in American courts.

Under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, diplomats serving abroad are legally bound to respect the laws of the country to which they are accredited. But they also have immunity from prosecution if those laws are broken.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns lamented as "a terrible tragedy that a young 16-year-old woman was killed in such a manner and killed in such a crime....We have great sympathy for the family of the young woman and we extend our condolences to her family and to her friends."
The United States expressed "very, very serious concern" to the Georgian ambassador about the accident, he added.
But Burns defended diplomatic immunity which "has existed as a concept for literally thousands of years" and has been practiced in the United States since 1790.

According to State Department records, few foreign diplomats based in Washington and New York have been involved in serious crimes like Friday's crash. But there are "tens of thousands of violations by foreign diplomats of U.S. laws on an annual basis," such as parking violations, Burns said.
